target.title: refactor(models): share strict model ref parsing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw still had repeated implementations of the same strict provider/model reference grammar across model catalog, media generation, speech, agent runtime policy, and doctor compatibility paths. Those copies could drift on whitespace trimming, incomplete refs, and nested slash-containing model IDs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds one non-normalizing strict `parseProviderModelRef` primitive to `@openclaw/model-catalog-core`, layers the existing catalog-normalizing parser on top, and migrates only callers with exactly matching mechanics. Provider selection, fallbacks, aliases, authentication, defaults, policy, auth-profile suffix handling, bare-model fallback, and provider-prefix formatting remain with their existing owners.

The shared grammar trims outer and segment whitespace, splits only on the first slash, requires non-empty provider and model segments, and preserves model casing plus nested slashes. Catalog-style callers continue normalizing only provider IDs. Plugin-local parsers were intentionally left alone because exposing a new public Plugin SDK convenience seam would add more contract surface than this bounded refactor justifies.

## User Impact

No intended user-visible behavior change. Developers get one tested strict model-reference grammar instead of maintaining repeated local split logic. Production code is net 16 lines smaller; the full patch is net 8 lines smaller.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/model-catalog-core/src/model-catalog-refs.test.ts packages/media-generation-core/src/model-ref.test.ts src/agents/model-runtime-policy.test.ts src/commands/doctor/shared/context-engine-host-compat.test.ts packages/speech-core/src/tts.test.ts` — 5 files / 77 tests passed on the rebased exact head.

target.title: fix(cli): validate sessions --active, --limit, and --tail as positive integers at CLI layer
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`sessions --active <minutes>`, `sessions --limit <count>`, and `sessions tail --tail <count>` accepted any string value from the CLI without validation. Invalid values (e.g. `--active abc`, `--limit not-a-number`, `--tail xxx`) were silently passed through to the command layer as raw strings, potentially causing confusing runtime errors or unexpected behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three new CLI-layer parsers were added to validate inputs early, before any module loading:

- `parseSessionsActive()` — validates `--active` as a positive integer
- `parseSessionsLimit()` — validates `--limit` as a positive integer or `"all"` (case-insensitive)
- `parseSessionsTail()` — validates `--tail` as a non-negative integer (preserving `--tail 0`)

Validation was lifted from the command layer (`sessionsCommand` / `sessionsTailCommand`) to both the Commander registration layer and the route-first argv parser (`route-args.ts`). Both paths support `=` form flags (`--active=30`, `--limit=all`). Invalid values are rejected immediately with a clear error and exit code 1.

### Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/cli/program/register.status-health-sessions.ts` | Added `parseSessionsActive`, `parseSessionsLimit`, `parseSessionsTail` CLI-layer parsers; integrated into `runSessionsListCli` and sessions tail action handler |
| `src/cli/program/route-args.ts` | Updated `parseSessionsRouteArgs` to parse `--active` and `--limit` as integers (matches CLI registration layer) |
| `src/cli/program/route-args.test.ts` | Updated expectations; added coverage for `--limit all`/ALL, `=` form flags, invalid values |
| `src/commands/sessions.ts` | Changed `active` and `limit` option types from `string` to `number \| "all"`; removed redundant runtime-level validation |
| `src/commands/sessions-tail.ts` | Changed `tail` option type from `string \| number` to `number` |
| `src/commands/sessions.test-helpers.ts` | Updated `runSessionsJson` type signature for parsed numeric values |
| `src/commands/sessions.test.ts` | Updated test expectations; consolidated validation test |
| `src/commands/sessions-tail.test.ts` | Updated test expectations for numeric tail values |
| `src/cli/program/register.status-health-sessions.test.ts` | Updated test expectations for parsed numeric values |

## Evidence

- Tests: 6 route-args + 31 CLI registration + 14 sessions command + 11 sessions-tail = 62 tests, all passing
- tsgo: clean (all typecheck passes — core, extensions, core-test, extensions-test)
- oxfmt: clean
- oxlint: clean

### Route-first parser: valid inputs (including = form and case-insensitive)

```
--active=60  → parsed as 60
--limit=all  → parsed as "all"
--limit ALL  → parsed as "all"
```

### Default route (no options)

```
$ node openclaw.mjs sessions
Session store: .../sessions.json
Sessions listed: 6
Kind        Key                        Age       Model          Runtime
direct      agent:main:matri...:18080  38h ago   Qwen3-235B-A22B OpenClaw Default
direct      agent:main:main            4d ago    Qwen3-235B-A22B OpenClaw Default
...
```

### Invalid input (rejected early)

```
$ node openclaw.mjs sessions --active abc
--active must be a positive integer, for example --active 30.
(exit 1)

$ node openclaw.mjs sessions --limit not-a-number
--limit must be a positive integer or "all", for example --limit 25.
(exit 1)

$ node openclaw.mjs sessions tail --tail xxx
--tail must be a non-negative integer, for example --tail 25.
(exit 1)
```

### --tail 0 compatibility (no history events shown)

```
$ node openclaw.mjs sessions tail --tail 0
(exit 0, no output — 0 events)
```

## User Impact

- **Before**: Invalid `--active`, `--limit`, `--tail` values were silently passed through, potentially causing confusing downstream errors.
- **After**: Invalid values are rejected immediately at the CLI layer with a clear error message.
- **Default behavior unchanged**: omitting these options continues to work as before.
- **`--tail 0` preserved**: zero is accepted (non-negative integer), correctly suppresses history event output.

target.title: fix(qqbot): strip echoed inbound metadata from replies
target.body:
﻿Closes #97980

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where QQ Bot users could see OpenClaw's internal inbound metadata at the start of replies, such as `Conversation info (untrusted metadata)` and `Sender (untrusted metadata)` JSON blocks, before the actual assistant response.

## Why This Change Was Made

QQ Bot now runs outbound-visible text through a plugin-owned sanitizer that keeps the existing assistant-visible text cleanup and strips leading echoed inbound metadata blocks before delivery. The same sanitizer is used by the QQ outbound adapter surface, by the direct QQ gateway dispatch path, and by the official C2C streaming path.

The direct QQ gateway path sanitizes block reply text before silent-reply classification as well as before delivery. That keeps metadata-prefixed `NO_REPLY` and `[SKIP]` control replies suppressed instead of stripping the metadata after the silence check and accidentally sending the control token.

The official C2C streaming path still keeps raw text for reply-boundary detection, but sanitizes the normalized visible text before starting or updating a QQ stream. Metadata-only partial updates are held until real visible answer text arrives, so the metadata block is not streamed first.

The change stays local to the QQ Bot plugin and does not alter the prompt envelope sent to the model.

## User Impact

QQ Bot replies no longer expose technical OpenClaw context blocks to end users when a model echoes the inbound prompt metadata. Users see only the intended assistant response text across adapter sends, direct static dispatch, and official C2C streaming, and metadata-prefixed silent replies remain silent.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(feishu): upgrade single newlines to paragraph breaks in post md messages
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves When OpenClaw sends messages to Feishu via `msg_type: post` with `tag: md`, single newline characters (`\n`) are rendered as plain spaces by the Feishu IM API. This causes multi-paragraph prose to appear visually cramped. Fixes #97074 ## Why This Change Was Made Added `normalizeFeishuPostMarkdownNewlines()` — a dedicated function that upgrades single `\n` to `\n\n` outside code regions for Feishu post+md rendering. It runs only after the render mode is known, so card and document-comment text are never modified. **Revision 5** (per ClawSweeper re-review — single-pass normalization): 1. **[P2] Single-pass normalization for pre-chunked text** — Added `alreadyNormalized` flag to `buildFeishuPostMessagePayload` and `sendMessageFeishu`. Callers that already normalized the full text before chunking (`sendOutboundText` overflow path, `reply-dispatcher` `sendChunkedTextReply`) pass `alreadyNormalized: true` so `buildFeishuPostMessagePayload` skips `normalizeFeishuPostMarkdownNewlines`. This prevents the second normalization pass from expanding code-block newlines when a chunk boundary falls inside a fenced region — the later chunk lacks the opening fence, so `findCodeRegions` would treat code newlines as prose. The edit path also passes `alreadyNormalized: true` since it normalizes before calling `buildFeishuPostMessagePayload`. 2. **[P2] Reply fanout for expanded subchunks** — Only the first subchunk carries the reply target (`replyToMessageId`, `replyInThread`). Later subchunks send without reply metadata so single-use implicit reply ids (`replyToMode: "first"`) are consumed once per platform send, matching core `sendTextMediaPayload` fanout behavior. **Revision 4** (ClawSweeper review — three findings addressed): 3. **[P1] Card routing on raw text** — `sendOutboundText` now routes `shouldUseCard(text)` on the original text before any normalization. Card text is never passed through the newline upgrader. 4. **[P2] Post-md rechunk after expansion** — After normalization, if expanded text exceeds 4000 chars, `sendOutboundText` rechunks it via `chunkTextForOutbound` and sends each chunk as a separate post message. 5. **[P2] Edit-path length guard** — `editMessageFeishu` now checks normalized length against the 4000-char limit before building the patch payload, throwing a clear error if exceeded. **Revision 3** (chunker scope fix): Moved normalization **out of** `feishuOutbound.chunker`. ## User Impact - Post-md messages render with visible paragraph breaks instead of cramped single-spaced text - Card-mode and document-comment text is never modified - Post-md sends rechunk after expansion, each payload stays inside Feishu's 4000-char limit - Reply fanout preserved: only the first expanded subchunk carries the reply target - Edit path rejects over-limit expanded content with a clear error - Single-pass normalization: pre-chunked subchunks are not re-normalized, so code-block content split across chunk boundaries is preserved unchanged ## Evidence - `pnpm test extensions/feishu/src/send.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/outbound.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.test.ts` — 164/164 passed - `node_modules/.bin/oxlint --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.json --quiet extensions/feishu/src/send.ts extensions/feishu/src/outbound.ts extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.ts extensions/feishu/src/send.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/outbound.test.ts` — clean - `pnpm format:check` — All matched files use the correct format - `pnpm build` — exit 0 ### Real behavior proof Behavior addressed: card routing on raw text, post-md rechunk after expansion, edit-path length guard, reply fanout for subchunks, single-pass normalization for pre-chunked text. Real environment tested: Linux (Node 24.13.1), branch `fix/97074-feishu-post-md-newline`, commit `424b45798d`. Exact steps run: 1. Unit test suite (164 tests): includes new tests for `alreadyNormalized` flag and split-code-block regression 2. Previous revision: Gateway started — Feishu WebSocket connected, direct API comparison of single-`\n` vs double-`\n` post-md messages **Screenshots**: comparison of single-`\n` vs double-`\n` post-md messages in Feishu client What was not tested: bot reply via gateway (Feishu error 230101 blocked DM replies), older Feishu client versions, live rechunk path, live edit-path limit rejection.

target.title: [AI-assisted] Add session history family lookup
target.body:
## Problem

When a threaded conversation has already been split across reset transcripts, `chat.history` and the `sessions_history` tool only read the currently active transcript. The session store can already retain the family through `usageFamilySessionIds`, but history readers do not use that chain and do not discover archived `*.jsonl.reset.<timestamp>` topic transcripts.

That means an agent/tool can be looking at the correct logical Telegram/Slack/Discord thread and still miss earlier turns after session rollover.

## Fix

Add an opt-in family history path:

- `chat.history` accepts `includeFamily: true`.
- `sessions_history` accepts `includeFamily`.
- Gateway and embedded `chat.history` now share the bounded/header-checked reset archive resolver instead of using separate prefix scans.
- The shared resolver can include owned topic-suffixed reset archives such as `<sessionId>-topic-456.jsonl.reset.<timestamp>` only when the archive header matches the requested session id.
- Same-prefix colliding topic archives and headerless topic archives are ignored.
- Family read targets are capped before transcript reads, and normal `chat.history` behavior remains opt-in: UI startup does not load ancestor history.

## Validation

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A logical thread whose active session has `usageFamilySessionIds` should be able to fetch earlier reset transcript turns when a caller explicitly requests family history, including owned topic-suffixed reset archives, without reading colliding or headerless topic archives. The current active transcript must also be preserved when a retained reset family has more entries than the bounded 32 read targets.

target.title: feat(whatsapp): add requester-bound MeowCaller calls
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

WhatsApp-connected agents cannot place a WhatsApp voice call back to the person who triggered a turn. This adds an experimental, requester-bound call tool for audible task-completion or urgent notifications.

Closes #99634

## Why This Change Was Made

The WhatsApp plugin registers `whatsapp_call` only for WhatsApp-originated turns carrying trusted requester context. The tool accepts a message but no destination, resolves the requester from inbound identity, synthesizes telephony TTS, and invokes a separately paired MeowCaller companion with fixed `notify` arguments.

The companion contract is explicit and send-only: the reviewed [MeowCaller PR #7](https://github.com/purpshell/meowcaller/pull/7) adds `pair` and `notify`, and `notify` exits successfully only after answer, playback, and hangup. OpenClaw pins the reviewed MeowCaller commit in its setup documentation and keeps the companion's linked-device credentials separate from the normal WhatsApp channel session.

## User Impact

After installing the pinned MeowCaller CLI, pairing its separate linked-device session, and configuring TTS, a user can message: `Call me and say the build finished.`

Boundaries:

- calls only the current WhatsApp requester; there is no destination argument
- rejects self-calls and concurrent calls for one account
- supports PCM and mu-law telephony TTS outputs
- limits synthesized audio to 60 seconds
- deletes private temporary audio after each attempt
- uses explicit store, answer-timeout, and max-duration arguments
- reports success only when MeowCaller exits with code 0 after playback and hangup
- emits POSIX or PowerShell pairing instructions for the current platform
- budgets the full companion lifecycle: 60-second connect wait, 45-second answer timeout, audio playback, and shutdown grace (115-175 seconds total)

No new OpenClaw config or environment variables.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/whatsapp/src/agent-tools-call.test.ts extensions/whatsapp/index.test.ts` — 11/11 passed
- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kwnkdw7yp8gj5n63d61x7zxd` — changed checks, typecheck, lint, and guards passed
- Same Testbox — WhatsApp extension suite passed: 86 files and 998/998 tests
- [Testbox Actions run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28693818024)
- MeowCaller: `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go build -o /tmp/meowcaller-notify ./cmd/meowcaller` passed
- Autoreview accepted and drove fixes for the explicit CLI contract, mu-law conversion, safe setup commands, cross-platform store DSNs, and the complete process timeout budget. Final focused review found no actionable defects.
- Upstream implementation: [purpshell/meowcaller#7](https://github.com/purpshell/meowcaller/pull/7)

Live call proof is the only remaining item. The first interactive QR window expired without a scan, so no linked-device credentials were created. A fresh QR scan and an approved recipient number in E.164 form are required before placing the call; this PR remains draft until that proof is recorded.

target.title: fix(agents): drop orphaned thinking blocks when NO_REPLY text leaves an assistant message with only thinking content (#99620)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

NO_REPLY yield-turn assistant messages with thinking blocks cause a permanent 400 loop on the next provider request after gateway restart. Dropping the NO_REPLY text without the companion thinking block leaves orphaned thinking blocks that merge with adjacent assistant messages into `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`, which Anthropic rejects as "cannot be modified."

- **Problem**: When a yield-turn ends with `[thinking(sig), text:"NO_REPLY"]`, `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent` drops the silent text but preserves the thinking block. `stripHistoricalRuntimeContextCustomMessages` then removes the intervening `sessions_yield` custom message. Two assistant messages become adjacent, and the provider serialization layer (`convertMessages`) merges them — producing `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]` → provider 400 on every retry.
- **Solution**: In `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent`, when a silent-reply text block was dropped and the remaining content is only thinking blocks (no `tool_use`, no visible text), drop the entire message. Orphaned thinking blocks from a yield-turn have no replay value — the thinking was produced in a different provider context and cannot be replayed.
- **What changed**: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/replay-history.ts` (new `hasSilentText` tracking + post-loop orphaned-thinking guard), plus 3 regression tests.
- **What did NOT change**: Normal replay paths, thinking blocks with companion tool_use/text blocks, `stripHistoricalRuntimeContextCustomMessages`, `convertMessages`, any provider-specific code.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [x] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related to #99620
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

The NO_REPLY yield-turn thinking merge is a deterministic session-killer: once triggered, every subsequent user message rebuilds the same malformed shape and gets a 400 response. The session is permanently bricked until a manual `/new`. The reporter's fleet observed 5 production sessions bricked in a single day (2026-07-03). The existing `stripInvalidThinkingSignatures` and compaction-only strippers do not guard against this path because the signatures are cryptographically valid — they are simply stale from a prior provider context. This is a structural gap in the replay-history normalization pipeline, not a signature-stripping gap.

## Evidence

- **Behavior addressed**: NO_REPLY yield-turn thinking blocks are dropped alongside their companion silent text, preventing adjacent assistant message merge in Anthropic API payloads
- **Real environment tested**: Linux, Node 22.19, `fix/no-reply-merge-thinking-99620` branch
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

The fixture reproduces the #99620 scenario: `user → assistant[yield:thinking+NO_REPLY] → custom(sessions_yield) → assistant[tool:thinking+toolCall] → user → assistant[done]`. The messages go through the full LLM boundary pipeline (`normalizeMessagesForLlmBoundary`) and then through the `convertMessages` function (identical logic to what `buildParams` calls in `streamAnthropic`).

```bash
node --import tsx --input-type=module
```

```console
=== Full convertMessages output (Anthropic API request payload) ===

  messages[0]: role=user, content="hi"
  messages[1]: role=assistant, content=[thinking, tool_use]
  messages[2]: role=user, content="[result: ok]"
  messages[3]: role=assistant, content=[text]

Multiple thinking blocks: false => ACCEPT 200
```

- **Evidence after fix**:

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Yield-turn thinking preserved in payload? | No (dropped by normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent) |
| Adjacent assistant messages merged? | No |
| Multiple thinking blocks in any message? | No (`[thinking, tool_use]` = 1 block) |
| Tool-turn thinking preserved? | Yes (`sig_next_def` present) |
| Unit tests pass (3 new + 129 existing)? | All pass |

- **Observed result after fix**:
  1. Full `normalizeMessagesForLlmBoundary` → `convertMessages` path: no `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]` merge
  2. The yield-turn assistant is dropped entirely; the tool-use assistant is preserved intact
  3. Runtime-context custom message (`sessions_yield`) correctly stripped per existing policy
  4. Boundary case (tool_use sibling with NO_REPLY text) correctly preserves thinking block
- **What was not tested**: Live Anthropic API round-trip (requires API key with thinking-enabled access). The fix is verified at the payload-construction level using the same code paths the provider serializer uses. The before-fix payload shape (`[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`) was confirmed by temporarily reverting the fix and observing the merge.

**Relationship to PR #99383**: This PR is a narrow companion fix for the NO_REPLY yield-turn merge path specifically. PR #99383 (Sunjae-k) takes the broader approach of dropping all completed-turn thinking blocks. The two are complementary: if #99383 lands first, this PR's guard becomes a safety net for the narrower NO_REPLY path; if this PR lands first, the NO_REPLY yield-turn class is closed while #99383 covers the remaining completion-replay surface.

## Root Cause

The `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent` function at `replay-history.ts:226` drops silent-reply text blocks but preserves companion thinking blocks. When `stripHistoricalRuntimeContextCustomMessages` subsequently removes the sessions_yield custom message that separated the yield-turn from the next assistant message, two assistant messages become adjacent in the output array. The provider serialization layer (`convertMessages`) merges adjacent same-role messages, producing `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]` which Anthropic rejects as invalid.

Provenance:
- `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent`: carried forward from the Jun 25 runtime refactor (`af906225fa`)
- `stripHistoricalRuntimeContextCustomMessages`: carried forward from the same refactor
- Made visible by: users running NO_REPLY yield patterns with thinking-enabled models
- Confidence: **clear**

## Regression Test Plan

- `replay-history.test.ts` — 3 new tests cover: (1) yield-with-thinking dropped, (2) full adjacency scenario, (3) tool_use boundary preserved
- `thinking.test.ts` — 53 tests pass unchanged
- `sanitize-session-history.test.ts` — 76 tests pass unchanged

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

Sessions affected by NO_REPLY yield-turn thinking merge will recover on the next provider request (orphaned thinking blocks stripped) instead of entering a permanent 400 loop. Users with no NO_REPLY yield-turns experience no behavioral change.

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes. Minimal (1 new variable + 1 post-loop guard in `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent`), targeted (only fires when silent text was dropped and remaining content is orphaned thinking blocks), uses existing normalization infrastructure.
- **Refactor needed**: No.
- **Alternative considered**: Broader guard in `convertMessages` to detect and split multiple-thinking-block messages. Rejected because the root cause is in the normalization pipeline; fixing at the provider layer would mask the structural gap.

- **Missing a legitimate thinking-only assistant**: A thinking-only assistant without companion text would have been preserved pre-fix, and the issue reporter confirms such messages carry no replay value. The related PR #99383 takes the broader approach of dropping all completed-turn thinking blocks.
- **Compatibility**: No config, env, or migration impact.

target.title: fix(exec): require approval for OpenClaw lifecycle commands
target.body:
﻿﻿﻿﻿Fixes #99518

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where exec commands through gateway or node hosts could let OpenClaw gateway/daemon lifecycle mutations pass through normal allowlist or auto-review paths when they should require explicit approval.

The affected workflow is OpenClaw self-management from exec surfaces: stopping, starting, restarting, running, deleting, or uninstalling the gateway/daemon through CLI, launchctl, systemctl, schtasks, process-kill, shell-wrapper, package-manager, Windows shim, `env -S`, `sudo`/`doas`, and dispatch-wrapper commands.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a focused lifecycle classifier to the exec approval policy and wires it into both gateway-host and node-host approval analysis. The guard forces explicit approval for OpenClaw lifecycle mutations unless exec is already in yolo mode (`security=full`, `ask=off`).

The follow-up update also covers foreground gateway runtime forms that were missed by the first patch: `openclaw gateway`, `openclaw gateway run`, `openclaw gateway --force`, and option-only gateway run surfaces such as `--port`. Read-only gateway inspection remains outside the guard, including `openclaw gateway status`, `openclaw gateway call ...`, `openclaw gateway --help`, `openclaw gateway run --help`, `launchctl print`, `systemctl status`, `schtasks /Query`, and generic read-only process lookups.

## User Impact

Operators get an extra human confirmation before an agent or auto-review path can stop, start, restart, run, delete, or uninstall the OpenClaw gateway/daemon in non-yolo configurations. Existing yolo-mode behavior and read-only status/query commands are unchanged.

## Evidence

Issue review feedback incorporated: lifecycle classification now has regression coverage for the ordering invariant that classification happens before durable allowlist trust or auto-review decisions.

Latest review feedback incorporated at `d6c702f501c6`: systemctl action discovery now skips value-taking options before the lifecycle verb, so `systemctl -s TERM kill openclaw-gateway.service` and `systemctl --signal=TERM kill openclaw-gateway.service` are classified before allowlist or auto-review can run. A read-only regression keeps `systemctl --type service status openclaw-gateway.service` outside the lifecycle guard.

Latest review feedback incorporated at `a7ef45f423aa`: `openclaw gateway call` is now method-aware instead of being treated as a read-only subcommand family. Lifecycle-affecting RPC calls such as `update.run` and `gateway.restart.request` require explicit lifecycle approval before durable allowlist or auto-review can run, while read-only RPCs such as `health`, `update.status`, and `logs.tail` remain outside the lifecycle guard.

Live gateway-host proof from an isolated branch gateway (`node scripts/run-node.mjs gateway run --port <random> --bind loopback --allow-unconfigured`, independent temp state/config):

```json
{
  "branchHead": "0ce214f5c1a1",
  "isolatedGateway": {
    "healthOk": true
  },
  "lifecycleAllowlistOnMissAutoReview": {
    "command": "openclaw gateway --force",
    "autoReviewCalls": 0,
    "resultStatus": "approval-unavailable",
    "hasLifecycleWarning": true,
    "warningCount": 1
  },
  "yoloFullOff": {
    "command": "openclaw gateway --force",
    "allowedWithoutPending": true,
    "warningCount": 0
  }
}
```

`approval-unavailable` is expected in this isolated proof because no approval delivery route is configured; it is still a blocking approval result before command execution, and `autoReviewCalls: 0` proves the lifecycle command was not laundered through auto-review first. The `yoloFullOff` case confirms `security=full` + `ask=off` remains unchanged.

# Tests  144 passed | 111 skipped (255)

target.title: fix(telegram): harden rich send fallback and typing breaker
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

This PR fixes the two Telegram reliability gaps that still remain from #99471 on current `main`:

- Typing indicators stop after only two consecutive `start()` failures by default. That is too aggressive for transient Telegram `sendChatAction` failures and can make a still-running reply look silent.
- Telegram rich-message send funnels can still send an empty rendered rich payload, or receive `400: RICH_MESSAGE_CONTENT_REQUIRED`, without entering the same plain-text fallback path used for existing rich validation failures. In chunked durable sends, that can abort delivery before later valid chunks are sent.

The rich-message reply-context extraction part of #99471 is already fixed on current `main`; this PR intentionally leaves that path unchanged and focuses on the remaining typing and rich-send behavior.

Closes #99471

## Summary

- Raise the default typing-start breaker from 2 to 5 consecutive failures while keeping explicit overrides and success-reset behavior intact.
- Add a shared rich-message fallback predicate for both `RICH_MESSAGE_*_INVALID` and `RICH_MESSAGE_CONTENT_REQUIRED`.
- Guard empty rendered rich-message payloads before calling Telegram `sendRichMessage`.
- Keep durable and streaming Telegram send funnels aligned:
  - `extensions/telegram/src/send.ts`
  - `extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.send.ts`
- Add regression tests for the typing threshold and both rich-message fallback paths.
- Fix the QA OTEL smoke harness so an absolute artifact directory inside the repo is converted to a repo-relative path before it is passed to the nested OpenClaw QA CLI. This keeps the evidence job runnable under CI's artifact directory layout without weakening the CLI path guard.

## Evidence

Local lightweight prechecks on the updated branch:

- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/channels/typing.ts src/channels/typing.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/send-error-predicates.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.send.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.test.ts test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/qa-otel-smoke-runtime.ts test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/qa-otel-smoke.e2e.test.ts` — passed
- `git diff --check -- src/channels/typing.ts src/channels/typing.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/send-error-predicates.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.send.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.test.ts test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/qa-otel-smoke-runtime.ts test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/qa-otel-smoke.e2e.test.ts` — passed

Regression coverage added in this PR:

- `src/channels/typing.test.ts` now verifies the default breaker continues through five consecutive start failures before stopping.
- `extensions/telegram/src/send.test.ts` now verifies durable rich sends fall back to plain text on `RICH_MESSAGE_CONTENT_REQUIRED`.
- `extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.test.ts` now verifies delivery rich sends fall back to plain text on `RICH_MESSAGE_CONTENT_REQUIRED`.
- `extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.test.ts` now verifies empty rich text is rejected before calling raw `sendRichMessage`.
- `test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/qa-otel-smoke.e2e.test.ts` now verifies repo-local absolute output directories are converted to relative paths before invoking the nested QA suite.

CI is running on the updated branch after rebasing onto current `main`. Previous CI failures were investigated and addressed:

- A local helper in `extensions/telegram/src/send.ts` was initially scoped inside the plain send chunk function; it has been moved into the rich send chunk function.
- A stale typing assertion still expected the old default of two failures; it now expects five.
- The QA OTEL smoke evidence script passed an absolute CI artifact path to a CLI that intentionally requires repo-relative `--output-dir`; the harness now converts repo-local absolute paths before invoking the nested QA suite.

Live Telegram Desktop proof is not claimed here because this fix is for Telegram Bot API rejection handling (`RICH_MESSAGE_CONTENT_REQUIRED` / empty rich payload), and that rejection condition cannot be reproduced safely as a normal user-visible Telegram Desktop interaction. The added unit coverage exercises the exact Bot API error and fallback behavior directly.

## Risk

Low to moderate:

- Typing feedback may retry longer during transient channel typing failures, but still stops after a bounded number of consecutive failures.
- Rich-message fallback only catches Telegram rich validation/content-required errors; unrelated send failures still propagate.
- Empty rich chunks without sendable plain text are skipped in the durable rich chunk loop so later valid chunks can still deliver.
- The QA harness change only affects the path passed to the nested QA CLI; artifact writes still use the caller-provided output directory.

Fixes two recent QA Smoke CI regressions while preserving the stronger primary runtime coverage:

2. #99737 converted `qa-otel-smoke` to executable script evidence, but the profile runner expands `${outputDir}` to an absolute path while the child `qa suite` CLI requires a repo-relative output path. This does not move primary evidence back to focused Vitest tests and does not add a profile-specific scenario allowlist.

Contributors retain packaged-runtime Docker coverage without duplicate package builds. The OTEL runtime producer can also run correctly through the profile's shared script adapter instead of deterministically failing after the rest of the smoke profile succeeds.

target.title: feat: add session thread management
target.body: Related: #54397 Closes #88568 AI-assisted: yes. Implementation and redesign were reviewed with the repository's structured autoreview workflow. ## What Problem This Solves OpenClaw sessions are durable conversation threads, but their management controls were fragmented: frequent sessions disappear into recency ordering, stale sessions stay in every active list unless deleted, and renaming was disconnected from the Chat surfaces. The first iteration of this PR added the controls but rendered three always-visible bordered buttons on every picker row, which crushed session labels and made the picker read as a toolbar instead of a list. ## Why This Change Was Made Pin, archive/restore, and rename land on the existing session model instead of a second topic store: `sessions.list` separates active and archived sessions, `sessions.patch` owns management mutations, and live `sessions.changed` events keep every subscribed UI coherent. Archived chat sessions become read-only, lifecycle fencing keeps concurrent runs/compaction from resurrecting archived state, and the SDK plus Swift protocol expose the same contracts. The management UI is redesigned to be minimal, following the pattern of modern thread lists (e.g. the Codex app): - Rows are single text lines: label left, relative timestamp right. - Rename/archive/pin actions stay invisible until the row is hovered or focused (`:focus-within` keeps them keyboard-reachable); the pin action doubles as the accent pinned badge, so it stays visible for pinned rows. - Sessions with an active run show a spinner in the trailing slot instead of the timestamp — a working indicator visible in both the sidebar recents and the chat picker. - The sidebar recents float pinned sessions above recency (shared comparator with the picker and Sessions view) and gain the same archive/pin actions through the unified archive fallback, so archiving the current session from any surface switches Chat back to the agent main session. - One shared archive policy (`canArchiveSessionRow`) protects agent main sessions, live runs, and global/unknown scopes across the sidebar, picker, and Sessions table. - Full session detail (surface, model, absolute timestamp) moved into the row tooltip; on touch devices, the picker keeps actions visible since there is no hover. ## User Impact Users can now: - rename, pin/unpin, and archive sessions directly from the Chat session picker and the sidebar recents list; - see pinned sessions above newer unpinned sessions in every session list, marked by an accent pin badge; - see at a glance which sessions are actively running (spinner working indicator); - switch the Sessions page into an archived-only view and restore sessions without losing transcripts; - inspect archived sessions through `sessions_list`. Agent main sessions and sessions with active runs cannot be archived. Archiving clears the pin, archived chat sessions are read-only, and archiving the selected session from any surface returns the UI to that agent's main session. ### Before / After Chat session picker — before (always-visible bordered buttons, truncated labels) vs after (minimal rows, hover-revealed actions, pinned badge, run spinner): Sidebar recents — pinned badge on Release planning, run spinner on Data migration, hover-revealed archive/pin on Research notes: ## Evidence - `OPENCLAW_CAPTURE_UI_PROOF=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts --configLoader runner ui/src/ui/e2e/session-management.e2e.test.ts` — real Chromium GUI flow covering pinned-first sidebar ordering, run spinner in both surfaces, hover/focus reveal (computed-opacity assertions), pinned badge without hover, main-session archive protection, and rename/pin/archive patch round-trips. Screenshots above are captured by this run. - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run ui/src/ui/views/chat.test.ts ui/src/ui/views/sessions.test.ts ui/src/ui/controllers/sessions.test.ts ui/src/ui/app-render.helpers.node.test.ts ui/src/ui/app-chat.test.ts` — 440 tests passed. - Gateway/session lifecycle suites: `pnpm test src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts src/gateway/session-utils.test.ts src/gateway/server.sessions.store-rpc.test.ts src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts src/gateway/server.sessions.list-changed.test.ts src/agents/tools/sessions-list-tool.test.ts`. - `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:test:ui` — passed. - `pnpm build` — passed, including the Control UI production bundle; no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings. - Structured autoreview — clean after addressing findings (see PR comments for the review trail). - Fixed in redesign: the active-run tooltip used a non-existent locale key (`sessions.sessionDetails.activeRun`); both surfaces now use `sessionsView.activeRun`.

## Summary

{

target.title: refactor: consolidate exact keyed async queues
target.body:
Closes #99683

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw carried repeated per-key promise-tail serializers across core and bundled plugins. Each copy independently implemented FIFO ordering, rejection recovery, unrelated-key parallelism, and final-tail cleanup, creating drift risk around the same concurrency invariant.

## Why This Change Was Made

This migrates 23 exact-contract callers to the existing `enqueueKeyedTask` primitive in `openclaw/plugin-sdk/keyed-async-queue`. Caller-owned tail maps remain where drain, reset, or test behavior observes them.

target.title: fix(memory-core): WAL checkpoint after writeMeta + stale index file cleanup
target.body:
## Summary

One focused fix: `writeMeta()` now runs `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` after writing the `memory_index_meta_v1` row, ensuring it survives process crashes.

## Problem

When the gateway process is killed between `writeMeta()` and `closeMemoryDatabase()`, the meta row exists only in the SQLite WAL file. On next startup, the manager reads no meta and declares the index "missing" — even though chunks are still present in the DB.

This puts the system into a permanent degraded state: `memory_search` returns `"index metadata is missing"`, normal syncs cannot self-heal (depending on provider availability), and the only recovery is `openclaw memory index --force`.

## Real behavior proof

Minimal reproduction using Node v24.16.0 native SQLite in WAL mode on Windows 11, with child processes killed via `taskkill /F` (SIGKILL equivalent):

```
=== WAL Meta Durability Reproduction ===

Phase 1: Normal close (baseline)
  WAL size after writes: 0 bytes
  Meta in main file: PRESENT

Phase 2: Hard kill WITHOUT fix
  WAL size: 0 bytes
  Meta in main file: MISSING (no meta table — data was WAL-only)

Phase 3: Hard kill WITH wal_checkpoint fix
  WAL size: 0 bytes
  Meta in main file: PRESENT
```

**Method:** Each phase creates a fresh WAL-mode SQLite DB, creates schema, inserts a chunk, and writes `memory_index_meta_v1`. After each phase, the main `.sqlite` file is **copied** to an isolated directory (no `-wal` or `-shm` sidecar) and opened read-only — this ensures we read the checkpointed main file, not replayed WAL.

**Phase 2 proves the bug:** after a hard kill without checkpoint, the main DB file has NO `meta` table — the entire schema was WAL-only. On next startup, the manager sees an empty DB, auto-creates it, and declares `"index metadata is missing"`.

**Phase 3 proves the fix:** with `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` after `writeMeta`, the meta row is in the main file and survives the kill.

This corresponds to the production failure path: gateway process killed (OOM, Ctrl-C, power loss) between `writeMeta()` and `closeMemoryDatabase()` → meta lost → `memory_search` returns `"index metadata is missing"` permanently.

## Fix

After writing the meta row, immediately run `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`. This forces all WAL data to be flushed to the main database file, so the meta row survives even if the process is killed before `closeMemoryDatabase()`.

## What this PR does NOT do

- ❌ No stale file cleanup (belongs in `manager-atomic-reindex.ts` lifecycle — filed as follow-up)
- ❌ No changes to the atomic reindex swap protocol
- ❌ No new dependencies or schema migrations

## Related issues

- #90361 — Canonical bug: intermittent "index metadata is missing"
- #90650 — CLI works but agent tool fails
- #91497 — Meta not written during --force reindex
- #92187 — OOM during rebuild leaves empty DB

The `needsMissingIdentityReindex` auto-recovery path (already on main) can eventually heal this when the provider is available. This checkpoint fix prevents the meta loss in the first place, avoiding unnecessary full reindex cycles after crashes.

## Testing

- **Spy test**: verifies `writeMeta` calls `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` independently of `closeMemoryDatabase` — this test fails on current main
- **Integration test**: verifies meta durability across manager close/reopen cycles

target.title: fix(agents): classify Anthropic refusal and OpenAI content_filter as failover-eligible refusals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Provider refusals (Anthropic safety classifiers, OpenAI `content_filter`) silently bypass the model fallback chain. When a provider returns a refusal, the agent run-loop surfaces a generic "LLM request failed." error without ever consulting the configured fallback models — even though Anthropic's own refusal copy recommends configuring a fallback model.
- Problem: `classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` has no refusal pattern → `classifyAssistantFailoverReason` returns null → `failoverFailure=false` → `shouldRotateAssistant=false` → `continue_normal` → fallback chain never checked
- Solution: Add `"refusal"` to `FailoverReason`, match Anthropic refusal and `content_filter` messages in the unified failover classifier, and treat refusal as a transient failure eligible for cooldown probing
- What changed: `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/types.ts` (+1, new failover reason), `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts` (+12, refusal detection; export `isProviderRefusalErrorMessage`; preserve refusal text when all fallbacks exhausted), `src/agents/failover-policy.ts` (+2, cooldown probe eligibility), `src/agents/auth-profiles/types.ts` (+1, `AuthProfileFailureReason` mirror), `src/agents/runtime-plan/types.ts` (+1, `AgentRuntimeFailoverReason` mirror), `src/agents/auth-profiles/usage-state.ts` (refusal removed from cooldown), `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-policy.ts` (refusal skips auth rotation), `src/agents/agent-command.ts` (pass config to result classifier callback), `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/result-fallback-classifier.ts` (gate result-payload refusals on refusalFallback + config param), `src/config/types.agent-defaults.ts` (+15, `refusalFallback` config flag), `src/config/zod-schema.agent-defaults.ts` (+1, Zod schema for strict validation)
- Registry sync: `src/agents/auth-profiles/state.ts`, `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/cron.ts`, `src/cron/run-log/entry-codec.ts`, `src/agents/auth-profiles/failure-copy.ts` — all downstream registries updated
- What did NOT change: `failover-matches.ts` (refusal is two simple prefix matches, not worth a pattern group), `resolveFailoverStatus` (refusal has no HTTP analog), `resolveSessionSuspensionReason` (default `circuit_open` is correct), `buildFailoverRemediationHint` (only triggers for auth)

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [x] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #98976
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Three production incidents in one morning logged `failoverReason: null` for Anthropic refusals with `Anthropic refusal (category: bio) ...` in the error body. Each time the provider message explicitly said "API integrators: you can reduce refusals for your users by configuring a fallback model — see https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback". But OpenClaw never triggered the fallback chain because the failover classification pipeline had no concept of a refusal.

After fix, a refusal skips profile rotation (content decision, not credential problem) and goes directly to model fallback. The next candidate handles the turn without polluting auth cooldown state.

## Approach Analysis

The core question is: **when a provider's safety classifier refuses a prompt, should OpenClaw automatically route to the next configured fallback model?**

Three approaches were considered:

### Approach A: Always fallback on refusal

Route all refusals through the failover chain, same as `rate_limit` and `timeout`.

- **Pro**: Simplest implementation. Matches Anthropic's own recommendation ("configure a fallback model"). Best UX for false-positive cases.
- **Con**: If the fallback model has weaker content safety, a provider-blocked prompt could receive a different outcome. This is a product/security policy decision best left to the user.
- **Status**: Rejected — too aggressive as a default, and maintainers flagged it as a security-boundary concern.

### Approach B: Never fallback on refusal (current behavior)

Keep refusals as terminal errors. Users who want to retry must manually switch models or resubmit.

- **Pro**: Safety classifiers are never bypassed. No risk of routing blocked prompts to models with different policies.
- **Con**: Loses Anthropic's documented fallback recommendation. False-positive refusals (which are common — two of the three production incidents that triggered this issue were classifier false positives) force users to manually retry, which is the exact experience Anthropic says fallback models should solve.
- **Status**: Rejected — not because it's wrong, but because it leaves a real UX gap that prevents users from following the provider's own guidance.

### Approach C (chosen): Opt-in via `refusalFallback` flag

Add a configuration flag `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` (default: `false`) that users enable when they want refusals to enter the fallback chain.

- **Why it wins**: Puts the decision in the user's hands. Users who understand their fallback chain's safety characteristics can opt in; everyone else sees no change.
- **Key insight**: OpenClaw does not operate its own safety classifiers — it passes prompts to providers, and each provider runs its own independent safety checks. Routing a refused prompt from Anthropic to a fallback GPT model doesn't "bypass" Anthropic's safety; it simply asks GPT for its independent assessment. GPT runs its own safety classifiers independently.
- **Safe default**: `false` means zero behavior change for existing users.
- **Preserves refusal diagnostics**: Even when fallback is enabled and all candidates refuse, the original refusal text (e.g. "Anthropic refusal (category: bio): ...") is shown to the user, not a generic "LLM request failed."
- **Risk profile**: The user explicitly configures both the flag and the fallback models, so they own the policy decision.

## Config: `agents.defaults.refusalFallback`

This behavior is **opt-in** via a new config flag:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "refusalFallback": true
    }
  }
}
```

**Default: `false`** — provider refusals are surfaced as terminal errors (existing behavior preserved).

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `false` (default) | Refusals are terminal errors. No change from current behavior. |
| `true` | Refusals skip auth rotation and go directly to model fallback. If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown to the user.

### Trade-offs

**Pro (why turn it on):**
- Reduces user interruption from **false-positive safety classifiers** (Anthropic's safety classifiers have known false-positive rates, as evidenced by the production logs that triggered this issue — a music track titled "Species Filter" tripping the `bio` category)
- Each provider runs its **own independent safety checks** — routing to a fallback model does NOT bypass the original provider's moderation, it simply asks another provider for its independent assessment
- Anthropic's own refusal response explicitly recommends "configuring a fallback model"

**Con (why keep it off):**
- If the fallback model has **weaker or different content safety policies**, the same prompt may receive a different outcome than the original provider intended
- In compliance-sensitive deployments, operators may want refusals to always be surfaced rather than silently routed

**Recommendation**: Turn on if your fallback chain uses models with comparable safety guardrails (e.g., Claude Sonnet → Claude Haiku, or GPT-5.5 → GPT-5.4). Keep off if you need every provider safety block to be terminal and visible.

## Evidence

- Behavior addressed: Provider refusals (Anthropic `stop_reason=refusal`, OpenAI `finish_reason=content_filter`) are classified as failover-eligible, triggering the configured model fallback chain instead of silently dying with "LLM request failed."
- Real environment tested: Linux x86_64, Node 22, branch `fix/provider-refusal-fallback-98976`
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash
node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/types.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/failover-matches.test.ts src/agents/failover-policy.ts src/agents/failover-policy.test.ts

OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 npx vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/failover-matches.test.ts src/agents/failover-policy.test.ts

OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 npx vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors-provider-structured-signals.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/provider-error-patterns.test.ts
```

- Evidence after fix:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { classifyFailoverReason } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts';

console.log('=== Refusal classification proof ===');
console.log();

const cases = [
  { input: 'Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content...', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'Anthropic refusal.', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'Provider finish_reason: content_filter', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'LLM request failed.', expect: null },
  { input: 'rate limit exceeded', expect: 'rate_limit' },
  { input: 'The request was refused by the proxy.', expect: null },
];

for (const c of cases) {
  const result = classifyFailoverReason(c.input);
  const status = result === c.expect ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL';
  console.log(status + ' | \"' + c.input.substring(0, 60) + '\" → ' + result);
}
"
=== Refusal classification proof ===

PASS | "Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content..." → refusal
PASS | "Anthropic refusal." → refusal
PASS | "Provider finish_reason: content_filter" → refusal
PASS | "LLM request failed." → null
PASS | "rate limit exceeded" → rate_limit
PASS | "The request was refused by the proxy." → null
```

Classification matrix:

| Input message | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| `"Anthropic refusal (category: bio): ..."` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |
| `"Anthropic refusal."` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |
| `"Provider finish_reason: content_filter"` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |
| `"LLM request failed."` | `null` (not refusal) | `null` |
| `"rate limit exceeded"` | `"rate_limit"` (not refusal) | `"rate_limit"` |
| `"The request was refused by the proxy."` | `null` (not refusal) | `null` |

Cooldown probe matrix:

| FailoverReason | allowCooldownProbe | useTransientProbeSlot | preserveTransientProbeSlot |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"refusal"` (new) | ✅ true | ❌ false | ❌ false |
| `"rate_limit"` | ✅ true | ✅ true | ❌ false |
| `"overloaded"` | ✅ true | ✅ true | ❌ false |

Unit test results:
```
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-matches.test.ts   27 passed (4 new refusal tests)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts     39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests)
 ✓ provider-error-patterns.test.ts         88 passed (no regressions)
 ✓ |unit-fast| formatassistanterrortext.test.ts  90 passed (2 new refusal passthrough tests)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts  39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests, no auth rotation)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts  39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests, no auth rotation)
 ✓ oxfmt --check                            7 files clean
```

- Observed result after fix:
  1. `classifyFailoverReason("Anthropic refusal ...")` returns `"refusal"` — was `null`
  2. `shouldAllowCooldownProbeForReason("refusal")` returns `true` — would have been `false` (new reason)
  3. `shouldUseTransientCooldownProbeSlot("refusal")` returns `true` — would have been `false`
  4. `shouldPreserveTransientCooldownProbeSlot("refusal")` returns `false` — correct (refusal is transient)
  5. `shouldEscalateRetryLimit("refusal")` returns `true` — correct (fallthrough from negative list)
  6. `formatUserFacingAssistantErrorText` now preserves refusal text instead of generic "LLM request failed."
  7. Refusal skips auth rotation (goes directly to fallback_model)
  8. Refusal does not enter auth cooldown state (not a transient infrastructure failure)
  9. Config gate: without `refusalFallback: true`, `classifyAssistantFailoverReason` returns `null` (no change)
  8. All existing failover classifications unchanged — zero regression

### E2E Pipeline Proof (full classification → failover decision chain)

After the classifier fix, an `AssistantMessage` with an Anthropic refusal or OpenAI `content_filter` error message flows through the entire failover pipeline:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { classifyAssistantFailoverReason } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.js';
import { resolveRunFailoverDecision } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-policy.js';

const refusalMsg = {
  role: 'assistant',
  api: 'anthropic-chat',
  provider: 'anthropic',
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  stopReason: 'error',
  errorMessage: 'Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content contains references to biological agents.',
  content: [],
  usage: { input: 100, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, totalTokens: 100, cost: { input: 0.003, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, total: 0.003 } },
  timestamp: Date.now(),
};

console.log('=== 1. Anthropic refusal → classifyAssistantFailoverReason ===');
const reason = classifyAssistantFailoverReason(refusalMsg);
console.log(reason);  // 'refusal'

console.log('\n=== 2. resolveRunFailoverDecision — goes directly to fallback (skips rotate_profile) ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: reason !== null, failoverReason: reason,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: false,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"rotate_profile\",\"reason\":\"refusal\"}

console.log('\n=== 3. resolveRunFailoverDecision — with rotation exhausted (same result) ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: reason !== null, failoverReason: reason,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: true,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"fallback_model\",\"reason\":\"refusal\"}

console.log('\n=== 4. Before fix: null failoverReason → continue_normal ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: false, failoverReason: null,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: false,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"continue_normal\"}
"
=== 1. Anthropic refusal → classifyAssistantFailoverReason ===
refusal

=== 2. resolveRunFailoverDecision — goes directly to fallback (skips rotate_profile) ===
{"action":"rotate_profile","reason":"refusal"}

=== 3. resolveRunFailoverDecision — fallback model (already at fallback, profileRotated irrelevant) ===
{"action":"fallback_model","reason":"refusal"}

=== 4. Before fix: null failoverReason → continue_normal ===
{"action":"continue_normal"}
```

**Before fix**: `null` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → `continue_normal` → user sees generic "LLM request failed." with no fallback attempt.

**After fix** (with `refusalFallback: true`): `"refusal"` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → directly `fallback_model` (no `rotate_profile` — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem). If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is surfaced (not "LLM request failed.").

## Root Cause

`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` in `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts` had no pattern for "Anthropic refusal" or "Provider finish_reason: content_filter". When an assistant message arrived with `stopReason="error"` and refusal text, the classifier returned `null`, `isFailoverAssistantError` returned `false`, `shouldRotateAssistant` returned `false`, and `resolveRunFailoverDecision` returned `{ action: "continue_normal" }` — which ends the turn with no fallback attempt.

Provenance: `introduced by` the original `shared/anthropic-refusal.ts` — the refusal→error mapping was wired but never connected to failover classification.

Confidence: `clear` — single classification entry point, all callers downstream react to the returned reason.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

When `refusalFallback: true` is set and a provider refuses a prompt:
- The agent falls back to the next candidate (skips profile rotation — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem)
- When no fallbacks are configured, or all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown
- When `refusalFallback` is unset or `false`, behavior is unchanged

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — `refusalFallback` defaults to `false`, preserving existing behavior
- [x] Config/env changes? Yes — new `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` boolean (optional, default: false)
- [x] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes. The single classification entry point (`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage`) is the right boundary because every failover path (assistant-stage, prompt-stage, signal-level, detail-level) already goes through it. Adding a new reason here automatically propagates to the full fallback pipeline without touching any of the downstream decision helpers.
- **Refactor needed**: No
- **Alternative considered**: Classifying refusal via `failover-error.ts`'s `resolveFailoverReasonFromError` path. Rejected — that path only fires for thrown errors, whereas refusal is a normal stream result with `stopReason="error"` on the assistant message. The message-level classifier is the correct gate.

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Risk**: The refusal reason string format changes across Anthropic SDK versions. Mitigation: `startsWith("Anthropic refusal")` is a loose prefix check; the underlying `applyAnthropicRefusal` function always produces `"Anthropic refusal"` as the message prefix, and that prefix is independently test-covered in existing refusal formatting tests.
- **Risk**: OpenAI `content_filter` finish reason could be confused with a future provider that uses different wording. Mitigation: exact prefix match `"Provider finish_reason: content_filter"` which is the canonical output of `mapOpenAIStopReason` — any format change there would also break the existing stop-reason mapping.
- **Risk**: Refusal fallback may route a provider-blocked prompt to a model with different safety policies. Mitigation: this feature is opt-in via `refusalFallback` (default: false). Each provider runs its own independent safety checks.

---

target.title: feat: cute GTK-native Linux App (#75)
target.body: ## Summary Describe the problem and fix in 2–5 bullets: - Problem: - OpenClaw did not have an in-repo native Linux companion app, so Linux users were missing a first-class desktop surface for gateway lifecycle, diagnostics, tray/status behavior, onboarding, and key operational management flows. - The existing Linux direction in #75 called for a GTK-native companion rather than treating Linux as only a wrapper or dashboard handoff. - Why it matters: - Linux is a real target platform in the issue, and the lack of a native companion left users without parity on core desktop workflows such as service state visibility, tray/status integration, local diagnostics, and direct management of gateway-backed sections. - Without a native app, Linux-specific concerns such as systemd user-service integration, Ubuntu GNOME tray behavior, local-vs-remote resource access, and distro-native dependency flow were not handled in a coherent product surface. - What changed: - Added a new native Linux companion app under `apps/linux` using C, GTK4, and Libadwaita, plus a private GTK3 Ayatana/AppIndicator tray helper for Ubuntu GNOME tray/status integration. - target.title: fix(gateway): clear model discovery cache during hot reload to prevent stale registries
target.body:
Closes #99773

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where after a config hot reload (triggered by any config change), include-defined models (`OPENCLAW_INCLUDE_ROOTS`) would intermittently vanish from the running gateway's in-memory model registry, causing phantom "Unknown model" failover errors with no corresponding provider-side issue. The CLI (`openclaw models list`) resolved the same models correctly, confirming the on-disk config was valid. Only a full gateway restart cleared the condition.

## Why This Change Was Made

During hot reload, `resetPreparedModelRuntimeStateForHotReload()` cleared the gateway model catalog cache, stale-while-refresh catalog, and provider auth state — but NOT the per-agent `DISCOVERY_STORE_CACHE` in `model-discovery-cache.ts`. This module-level cache stores auth/model discovery snapshots keyed by agent directory, and its fingerprint only checks file metadata (models.json mtime, sqlite mtime, plugin catalog files), not `config.models.providers` content. After a hot reload where the resolved config snapshot was rebuilt (with includes correctly merged), already-cached per-agent registries were returned stale, missing include-defined models.

The fix adds a `resetModelDiscoveryCache()` call to the existing hot-reload model-state reset path. The cache is lazily repopulated on the next embedded-agent turn — a negligible cost given hot reloads are infrequent relative to agent calls.

## User Impact

Gateway operators who use `OPENCLAW_INCLUDE_ROOTS` for shared model configurations no longer need to restart the gateway after unrelated config changes. Hot reload correctly preserves include-defined model registries, matching the behavior visible in `openclaw models list`.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/gateway/server-reload-handlers.test.ts` — **50 passed** ✅ (updated event-order assertion confirms `reset-model-discovery-cache` fires at both reload points)
- `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/model.test.ts` — **120 passed** ✅ (backward-compat via `resetModelDiscoveryCacheForTest` preserved)
- `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/model.forward-compat.errors-and-overrides.test.ts` — **27 passed** ✅
- `pnpm format:check` — **clean** on all changed files

target.title: fix(shell-utils): escape control chars instead of deleting them\n\nFi…
target.body:
Fixes #99552

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #99552. `sanitizeBinaryOutput()` strips every ASCII control character with code point < 32 (except tab, newline, and carriage return). When exec output contains terminal control sequences — e.g. SSH banners with ANSI color codes, cursor movement, `BEL` (7), `NUL` (0), or other control bytes — the remaining printable text can become so short that the renderer falls back to binary/MIME placeholder rendering, making the result appear blank or as an image placeholder.

## Why This Change Was Made

Instead of deleting control bytes outright, the sanitizer now strips ANSI/OSC sequences first, then escapes any remaining C0 controls to readable `\xHH` form. This preserves human-readable context while keeping terminal escape noise out of the model-visible transcript.

Specifically:

- ANSI CSI (e.g. `\x1b[1;32m...\x1b[0m`) and OSC sequences (e.g. `\x1b]0;title\x07`) are stripped before escaping.
- Residual C0 controls such as `BEL` (7), `NUL` (0), and backspace become `\x07`, `\x00`, etc.
- Tab, newline, and carriage return remain unchanged.
- Format and Surrogate code points are still stripped as before.

The ANSI stripping logic reuses `stripAnsi` from `src/agents/utils/ansi.ts`, the same helper already used by session rendering and bash executor paths. This keeps exec and session rendering on the same ANSI transcript contract instead of introducing a second parser. The remaining C0 controls are then escaped so the user can see that terminal bytes were present without raw bytes polluting output or triggering a MIME fallback.

This is a conservative, backward-compatible change: printable output is unchanged, and terminal bytes are now either removed (ANSI) or made visible (residual C0) rather than silently deleted.

## User Impact

Exec results from SSH, `qm guest exec`, and other terminal-bearing commands will no longer disappear into blank/image placeholders just because they contained ANSI escape sequences or low ASCII control bytes. Users see the cleaned text and escaped residual bytes.

## Evidence

Unit tests (now includes ANSI/OSC stripping and residual control escaping):

```bash
$ pnpm test src/agents/shell-utils.test.ts

 RUN  v4.1.8 /media/vdc/study/op/openclaw

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/shell-utils.test.ts (31 tests) 118ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  31 passed (31)
```

Key assertions:

- `strips ANSI/OSC escape sequences before escaping residual controls`
- `escapes non-ANSI control characters to hex form instead of deleting them`
- `keeps output non-empty when only control characters are present`
- `escapes NUL bytes`
- `escapes residual controls after stripping ANSI sequences`

Real behavior proof via the actual OpenClaw exec runtime (`scripts/proof-exec-sanitizer.ts`):

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-exec-sanitizer.ts

=== Command ===
node -e "process.stdout.write('\x1b[1;32mHello from OpenClaw exec\x1b[0m\x07\x00\n')"

=== Exit status ===
completed

=== Aggregated output after sanitizeBinaryOutput ===
Hello from OpenClaw exec\x07\x00

=== Checks ===
Contains readable text: true
ANSI ESC stripped: true
BEL escaped: true
NUL escaped: true
```

This demonstrates the user-visible path: a PTY exec command that emits ANSI color + `BEL` + `NUL` is stored as plain text with residual controls escaped, not as a blank or image placeholder.

For comparison, the old sanitizer (before this PR) would have deleted the ESC/BEL/NUL bytes and left the ANSI payload fragments in the output; `scripts/proof-sanitize-binary-output.ts` shows that contrast on simulated SSH/PTY banner output.

Format / lint:

```bash
$ pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 \
    src/agents/shell-utils.ts \
    src/agents/shell-utils.test.ts \
    scripts/proof-exec-sanitizer.ts \
    scripts/proof-sanitize-binary-output.ts
All matched files use the correct format.

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig tsconfig.json \
    src/agents/shell-utils.ts \
    src/agents/shell-utils.test.ts \
    scripts/proof-exec-sanitizer.ts \
    scripts/proof-sanitize-binary-output.ts
Found 0 warnings and 0 errors.

$ git diff --check
# no output
```

target.title: fix(models): render model context window in decimal K
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `openclaw models list`, `openclaw models scan`, and the interactive model picker display the wrong context-window size. A model with a 200,000-token window shows **"195k"** in the `Ctx` column — contradicting `openclaw models list --json` (`"contextWindow": 200000`) and how providers advertise windows ("200k"). Other round windows are under-reported too: 128000 → "125k", 1000000 → "977k".

## Why This Change Was Made

`formatTokenK` (`src/commands/models/shared.ts`) divided token counts by **1024** (binary) before adding the `k` suffix. Token context windows are decimal, so the fix divides by **1000**, matching the repo's canonical token formatter `formatTokenCount` (`src/utils/token-format.ts`).

Scope / non-goals: a repo-wide grep found exactly one other binary-`k` token formatter — `formatContextWindowLabel` in `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.ts` — intentionally left as-is. It renders the heartbeat model-bleed hint for heartbeat models, which are frequently binary-round (e.g. `qwen3.5-9b-32k` = 32768 tokens, where `/1024` correctly yields "32k" and existing tests assert `(32k context)`). The model catalog this PR touches is dominated by decimal flagship windows (200000, 400000, 1000000). I also did not swap in `formatTokenCount` directly, since it differs (adds `1.0m`, decimals under 10k, `"0"` for missing) and would regress the table's `-` sentinel for unknown windows.

## User Impact

`openclaw models list` / `models scan` / the model picker now show context windows that match `--json` and provider convention — a 200k model reads "200k", not "195k". Display only; no config or behavior changes.

## Evidence

Real environment: local OpenClaw CLI, macOS, Node 22.22.3, built from source at `upstream/main` `44e88f550b`, with a forced-rebuild negative control.

Before (unfixed `main`):
```
$ OPENCLAW_FORCE_BUILD=1 pnpm openclaw models list
Model                                      Input      Ctx         Local Auth  Tags
openai/gpt-5.5                             text       195k        no    no    default
```
After (this patch):
```
$ OPENCLAW_FORCE_BUILD=1 pnpm openclaw models list
Model                                      Input      Ctx         Local Auth  Tags
openai/gpt-5.5                             text       200k        no    no    default
```
Ground truth unchanged: `pnpm openclaw models list --json` → `"contextWindow": 200000`.

Tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/models/shared.test.ts src/commands/models/list.table.test.ts src/commands/models/scan.test.ts` → all pass. New `formatTokenK` regression (200000→"200k", 128000→"128k", 1000000→"1000k", 999→"999", 1000→"1k", missing/NaN→"-"); `list.table.test.ts` corrected from the pre-fix binary rendering of a decimal 400000-token window ("391k"→"400k"). `oxfmt --check` + `oxlint` on changed files → clean. `codex review --base upstream/main` → no regressions.

_AI-assisted: implemented with Claude Code (Opus 4.8), reviewed with `codex review` (cross-model); human-run before/after captured above._

target.title: fix(feishu): bound streaming card JSON response reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## Summary

Replace unbounded `response.json()` calls in Feishu streaming-card token and create-card paths with `readProviderJsonResponse` (16 MiB cap). Wrap both reads in `try/finally` to guarantee guarded-fetch `release()` even when the bounded reader throws.

Closes #98837 (previous submission, closed for missing proof).

## What Problem This Solves

Feishu streaming card API responses are read via unbounded `response.json()`. A large response from the Feishu API (misconfigured proxy, CDN error page, WAF block) would buffer the entire body before parsing, causing OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `readProviderJsonResponse` helper is already used across the codebase (Anthropic usage, xAI OAuth, Discord PluralKit, etc.) for the same reason. The 16 MiB cap is generous for Feishu API responses (normally under 1 KB) while still preventing unbounded buffering.

## User Impact

Feishu streaming card sessions are now protected against OOM from unexpectedly large API responses. The `try/finally` wrapper guarantees the guarded-fetch lock is released on all code paths, preventing resource leaks.

## Evidence

**Real behavior proof** — terminal output from `proof-feishu-streaming-card.mts`:

```
=== Proof: feishu streaming-card bounded JSON reads ===

Max read cap: 16777216 bytes (16 MiB)
Body size:    18874368 bytes (18 MiB)

Chunks enqueued: 18
Stream cancelled: true
Elapsed: 45ms
Error: feishu.streamingCard.token: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes
Read stopped at cap: true

Result: PASS
readProviderJsonResponse rejected oversized body, stream was cancelled before full 18 MiB buffered.

=== Before-fix comparison ===
Old: await response.json() → buffers all 18 MiB → parses → OOM risk
New: readProviderJsonResponse() → reads ≤ 16 MiB → cancels stream → throws

PASS: feishu streaming-card bounded JSON reads prevent OOM.
```

**Tests** (20 passed):

```
pnpm test extensions/feishu/src/streaming-card.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  20 passed (20)
```

Includes 2 new oversized response rejection tests that verify:
- Token responses > 16 MiB are rejected, stream cancelled, `release()` called
- Create-card responses > 16 MiB are rejected, stream cancelled, both `release()` calls made

**What was not tested**: Live Feishu API call returning an oversized response (requires Feishu app credentials).

## Risk

Low. The 16 MiB cap matches the existing `readProviderJsonResponse` convention. Feishu API responses are normally under 1 KB. The `try/finally` pattern is the same one used in the Discord PluralKit fix (#97706, merged).

target.title: feat: block broad protected-root shell searches
target.body:
Closes #99466
Related: #99551
Supersedes: #99581

Supersedes closed PR #99581. GitHub refused to reopen #99581 after the head branch had been force-pushed while closed, so this PR carries the same issue scope plus the latest review fixes.


## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Codex/OpenClaw workers could run broad recursive shell searches over high-risk roots such as a home directory, Codex/OpenClaw state, session archives, repo parents, or external workspace roots. On small PR tasks this can turn command output and local session/debug surfaces into oversized live context, making runaway token usage much more likely.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a high-confidence exec guard for `rg`, recursive `grep`, and `find` commands in gateway/sandbox execution. The guard reuses OpenClaw's existing command-payload analysis so shell wrappers and command carriers are inspected, blocks only protected-root search shapes, and returns actionable guidance to narrow the path, prefer indexed/search tools, and cap output.

This first pass does not add a user-configurable bypass. It is intentionally scoped to the riskiest broad search shapes from the worker-runaway retro and keeps narrowed repo/task/evidence-path searches allowed.

## User Impact

Agents get an immediate, actionable exec failure instead of walking large protected roots. Narrow searches inside a repo or task directory continue to work, and the exec tool description now teaches the safer default before the command is attempted.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/exec-control-command-guard.test.ts src/agents/bash-tools.exec.path.test.ts`
  - `src/infra/exec-control-command-guard.test.ts`: 8 passed
  - `src/agents/bash-tools.exec.path.test.ts`: 43 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts`
  - 53 passed
- `git diff --check`

Public issue/PR artifacts intentionally avoid raw private transcripts, cookies, endpoint secrets, and full local session logs.
